claim: Intermediate filament (IF) proteins, including nuclear lamins and cytoplasmic IF proteins, are essential cytoskeletal components of bilaterian cells.
source: Intermediate filament (IF) proteins, including nuclear lamins and cytoplasmic IF proteins, are essential cytoskeletal components of bilaterian cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about IF proteins in bilaterians.

claim: No cytoplasmic IF proteins have been convincingly identified in arthropods.
source: Despite their important role in protecting tissues against mechanical force, no cytoplasmic IF proteins have been convincingly identified in arthropods.
evidence: This claim is supported by the literature review and the authors' own comprehensive screening of arthropod genomes and transcriptomes.

claim: The ancestral cytoplasmic IF protein gene was lost in the entire panarthropod lineage rather than just the arthropod lineage.
source: Here we show that the ancestral cytoplasmic IF protein gene was lost in the entire panarthropod (onychophoran + tardigrade + arthropod) rather than arthropod lineage
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses showing all panarthropod IF proteins cluster within the lamin clade, not the cytoplasmic IF clade.

claim: Nuclear, lamin-derived proteins acquired new cytoplasmic roles at least three times independently in collembolans, copepods, and tardigrades.
source: nuclear, lamin-derived proteins instead acquired new cytoplasmic roles at least three times independently in collembolans, copepods, and tardigrades.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses showing independent clustering of these groups within the lamin clade and the absence of nuclear localization signals in specific proteins.

claim: Hypsibius dujardini has three IF protein genes.
source: Transcriptomic and genomic data revealed three IF protein genes in the tardigrade Hypsibius dujardini
evidence: This is directly supported by transcriptomic and genomic sequencing data.

claim: Cytotardin occurs exclusively in the cytoplasm of epidermal and foregut epithelia in H. dujardini.
source: one of which (cytotardin) occurs exclusively in the cytoplasm of epidermal and foregut epithelia
evidence: This is supported by immunolocalization experiments shown in the figures.

claim: Cytotardin forms belt-like filaments around each epithelial cell.
source: where it forms belt-like filaments around each epithelial cell.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy images.

claim: A lamin derivative has been co-opted to enhance tissue stability in tardigrades.
source: These results suggest that a lamin derivative has been co-opted to enhance tissue stability in tardigrades, a function otherwise served by cytoplasmic IF proteins in all other bilaterians.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic position of cytotardin within the lamin clade and its cytoplasmic localization in stress-bearing tissues.

claim: Tardigrades live in marine, freshwater and semi-aquatic/limno-terrestrial environments.
source: Tardigrades, also known as water bears, are microscopic invertebrates that live in marine, freshwater and semi-aquatic/limno-terrestrial environments (Kinchin, 1994; Nelson, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tardigrades have the ability to survive extreme conditions including exposure to space.
source: Although tardigrades have become renowned for their ability to survive extreme conditions (Møbjerg et al., 2011; Ramløv and Westh, 2001), including exposure to space (Persson et al., 2011; Rebecchi et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Little is known about the actual mechanisms that allow tardigrade cells to resist severe mechanical stress caused by desiccation and freezing.
source: only little is known about the actual mechanisms that allow their cells to resist severe mechanical stress caused by desiccation and freezing (Møbjerg et al., 2011; Ramløv and Westh, 2001; Wright, 2001; Tanaka et al., 2015; Yamaguchi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations indicating gaps in current knowledge.

claim: IF proteins are essential for stress resilience of cells.
source: The integrity and plasticity of tardigrade tissues might be achieved by specialised cytoskeletal components, such as IF proteins, which are known to be essential for stress resilience of cells (Herrmann et al., 2009; Coulombe and Wong, 2004; Kim and Coulombe, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on IF protein function.

claim: Lamins occur in most eukaryotes, including social amoebae and all metazoans.
source: While lamins, a group of IF proteins found in the nucleus, occur in most eukaryotes, including social amoebae (Krüger et al., 2012) and all metazoans (Dittmer and Misteli, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cytoplasmic IF proteins evolved from an ancestral lamin gene by duplication in the bilaterian lineage.
source: cytoplasmic IF proteins are thought to have evolved from an ancestral lamin gene by duplication in the bilaterian lineage (Erber et al., 1999; Herrmann and Strelkov, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published evolutionary studies.

claim: Cytoplasmic IF proteins are present in all bilaterian taxa excluding arthropods.
source: Genomic and biochemical studies have revealed that the cytoplasmic IF proteins are present in all bilaterian taxa excluding arthropods (Bartnik and Weber, 1989; Goldstein and Gunawardena, 2000; Erber et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic and biochemical studies.

claim: The apparent loss of cytoplasmic IF proteins in the arthropod lineage might correlate with the acquisition of an exoskeleton.
source: The apparent loss of cytoplasmic IF proteins in the arthropod lineage might correlate with the acquisition of an exoskeleton (Herrmann and Strelkov, 2011; Goldstein and Gunawardena, 2000; Erber et al., 1998), which provides mechanical support to the arthropod skin.
evidence: This is a hypothesis cited from the literature.

claim: H. dujardini shows only a limited ability to tolerate desiccation (anhydrobiosis).
source: Although this model tardigrade (Gabriel et al., 2007; Gross et al., 2015) shows only a limited ability to tolerate desiccation (anhydrobiosis)
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of this species.

claim: H. dujardini clearly survives immediate freezing (cryobiosis).
source: it clearly survives immediate freezing (cryobiosis; see Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Video 1 showing recovery after freezing.

claim: Transcriptomic analyses revealed only one putative IF protein transcript in each of five onychophoran species.
source: Our analyses revealed only one putative IF protein transcript in each of the five onychophoran species but three in H. dujardini.
evidence: This is based on transcriptomic sequencing and analysis.

claim: The three tardigrade IF proteins share a similar α-helical rod domain organization with three coiled coil-forming segments (coil 1A, coil 1B, coil 2).
source: According to sequence comparisons with well-characterized IF proteins from humans and the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, all corresponding proteins of the three identified genes share a similar α-helical rod domain organization with three coiled coil-forming segments (coil 1A, coil 1B, coil 2; Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2) (review Chernyatina et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and comparison with known IF proteins.

claim: The three tardigrade IF proteins possess highly conserved intermediate filament consensus motifs at the beginning and end of the rod domain.
source: This, in conjunction with the highly conserved intermediate filament consensus motifs (review Herrmann and Aebi, 2004) at the beginning and end of the rod domain of all three tardigrade proteins, classify them as intermediate filament proteins.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison with known IF consensus motifs.

claim: The three tardigrade IF proteins possess 42 residues in the coil 1B, a feature shared between all eukaryote lamins and protostome cytoplasmic IF proteins.
source: The three tardigrade IF proteins further possess 42 residues in the coil 1B (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) — a feature that is shared between all eukaryote lamins and protostome cytoplasmic IF proteins but that must have been deleted from the ancestral cytoplasmic IF protein gene in chordates (Herrmann et al., 2009; Peter and Stick, 2015).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison with other IF proteins.

claim: Lamin-2 possesses all major regions known from other eukaryote lamins, including the nuclear localization signal (NLS), the lamin-tail domain (LTD), and the carboxy-terminal CaaX motif.
source: One of them, which we named lamin-2, possesses all major regions known from other eukaryote lamins (Herrmann et al., 2009; Dittmer and Misteli, 2011; Burke and Stewart, 2013), including the nuclear localization signal (NLS) — which generally mediates the import of proteins into the nucleus (Mical et al., 2004) — the lamin-tail domain (LTD), and the carboxy-terminal CaaX motif (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and domain prediction.

claim: Lamin-1 lacks the CaaX box.
source: In contrast, the second tardigrade IF protein (named lamin-1) lacks the CaaX box
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cytotardin is missing the NLS, LTD, and CaaX motifs, indicating it may localize in the cytoplasm rather than the nuclear lamina.
source: whereas the third IF protein from H. dujardini is missing all three motifs, including the NLS, indicating this protein may instead localize in the cytoplasm rather than the nuclear lamina of H. dujardini cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of nuclear targeting sequences in the protein sequence.

claim: All identified tardigrade and onychophoran IF sequences cluster within the bilaterian lamin clade in phylogenetic analyses.
source: In our phylogenetic analyses, all identified tardigrade and onychophoran sequences cluster within the bilaterian lamin clade, whereas none of them groups with cytoplasmic IF protein-coding genes (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on maximum likelihood phylogenetic analyses.

claim: The three identified IF sequences of H. dujardini, together with two sequences from Milnesium tardigradum, form a strongly supported monophyletic clade of tardigrade lamins.
source: Surprisingly, the three identified IF sequences of H. dujardini, together with two sequences from Milnesium tardigradum, form a strongly supported monophyletic clade of tardigrade lamins (GTR+G: Bootstrap support BS=77, LG+G: BS=80) in our analyses (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analyses with bootstrap support values.

claim: There were at least two duplication events in the tardigrade lineage that gave rise to lamin-1, lamin-2 and cytotardin genes.
source: This implies that there were at least two duplication events in the tardigrade lineage that gave rise to lamin-1, lamin-2 and cytotardin genes
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic tree topology showing tardigrade IF proteins as a monophyletic group.

claim: The isomin sequence of the collembolan Isotomurus maculatus clusters with other identified collembolan transcripts within the clade of arthropod lamins.
source: Our results further show that the isomin sequence of the collembolan Isotomurus maculatus does in fact cluster with other identified collembolan transcripts (GTR+G: BS=74, LG+G: BS=70) within the clade of arthropod lamins (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2)
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analyses with bootstrap support.

claim: Isomin is not an ortholog of bilaterian cytoplasmic IF proteins.
source: These results clearly challenge the identity of isomin as a member of the bilaterian cytoplasmic IF protein clade (Mencarelli et al., 2011) and suggest that orthologs of genes encoding these proteins are entirely missing in arthropods, at least in those with known genomic sequences.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analyses contradicting a previous interpretation.

claim: Cytoplasmic IF protein genes were already lost in the panarthropod lineage.
source: our transcriptomic and genomic analyses, which included screening of the genome of the centipede Strigamia maritima (see Chipman et al., 2014), the water flea Daphnia pulex (see Colbourne et al., 2011), and more than 70 transcriptomes from hexapod species sequenced as part of the 1KITE project (Misof et al., 2014), strongly suggest that these genes were already lost in the panarthropod lineage, since all of these panarthropod IF proteins cluster within a well-supported monophyletic clade of bilaterian lamins (GTR+G: BS=84, LG+G: BS=76; Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on comprehensive genomic and transcriptomic screening combined with phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Lamin-1 and lamin-2 proteins both display a typical, lamin-like distribution within all nuclei.
source: As predicted, lamin-1 and lamin-2 proteins both display a typical, lamin-like distribution within all nuclei (Figure 4A–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunolocalization experiments.

claim: Lamin-1 is localised throughout the nucleoplasm.
source: While lamin-1 is localised throughout the nucleoplasm (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence microscopy.

claim: Lamin-2 is restricted to the nuclear periphery.
source: lamin-2 is restricted to the nuclear periphery (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence microscopy.

claim: There is a small overlap region between lamin-1 and lamin-2.
source: although there is a small overlap region between these two proteins (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown by double immunofluorescence labeling.

claim: The intranuclear distribution of lamin-1 corresponds to its lack of the CaaX motif.
source: The intranuclear distribution of lamin-1 corresponds to its lack of the CaaX motif, which is responsible for the association of lamins with the nuclear envelope (Kitten and Nigg, 1991).
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of the CaaX motif and the observed localization pattern.

claim: Cytotardin is not localised within the nucleus, but in the peripheral cytoplasm of all epidermal and foregut cells.
source: In contrast to the two lamins, cytotardin of H. dujardini is not localised within the nucleus, but in the peripheral cytoplasm of all epidermal and foregut cells, where it appears to be closely associated or aligned with the plasma membrane (Figure 4E–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunolocalization experiments.

claim: Cytotardin encircles the apical regions of cells in a belt-like, filamentous array.
source: In this setting, it encircles the apical regions of the cells in a belt-like, filamentous array (Figure 4E–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by confocal microscopy images.

claim: Cytotardin forms both short filaments and extensive cytoskeletal networks in transfected MCF-7 cells.
source: Immunofluorescence analyses using cytotardin antibody revealed that this protein is located exclusively in the cytoplasm of transfected MCF-7 cells, where it forms both short filaments and extensive cytoskeletal networks which most likely are homopolymeric (Figure 5A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transfection experiments and immunofluorescence microscopy.

claim: Cytotardin is not co-localised with desmoplakin in transfected MCF-7 cells.
source: Double labelling for cytotardin and desmoplakin, a desmosomal protein mediating membrane attachment of mammalian IF proteins (Simpson et al., 2011), shows that cytotardin occurs close to desmosomes but is not co-localised with desmoplakin (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is shown by double immunofluorescence labeling.

claim: Cytotardin and keratin-8 are not co-localised in transfected MCF-7 cells.
source: Our data show that these two proteins are not co-localised and that the endogenous keratin networks are displaced in cells with dense cytotardin arrays (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is shown by double immunofluorescence labeling.

claim: Cytotardin has an intrinsic ability to form homopolymeric filaments and cytoplasmic networks.
source: These findings strongly support an intrinsic ability of the cytotardin protein of H. dujardini to both form homopolymeric filaments and cytoplasmic networks — both properties that are functionally analogous to mammalian cytoplasmic IFs (Bohnekamp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the transfection experiments showing cytotardin can form networks independently of endogenous IF proteins.

claim: Cytotardin's belt-like arrays are confined to the ectodermal epithelia, including the epidermis, buccal tube, pharynx, and oesophagus.
source: Our data on tissue-specific distribution of cytotardin in H. dujardini further show that its belt-like arrays are confined to the ectodermal epithelia, including the epidermis, buccal tube, pharynx, and oesophagus (Figures 4E–G and 6A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunolocalization in whole-mount and sectioned specimens.

claim: The entire tardigrade body is ensheathed by a grid of belt-like filaments formed by the cytotardin protein.
source: Thus, the entire tardigrade body is ensheathed by a grid of belt-like filaments formed by the cytotardin protein, which retain their integrity even in contracted specimens (Figure 4E–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by whole-mount immunolabeling.

claim: The most prominent anti-cytotardin immunoreactivity is found in areas exposed to considerable physical stress in living specimens, including the bases of claws and the stylet apparatus.
source: The most prominent anti-cytotardin immunoreactivity is found in areas exposed to considerable physical stress in living specimens, including the bases of claws and the stylet apparatus (Figures 4F,G and 6B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunolocalization showing differential intensity of staining.

claim: Much of the resistance of the tardigrade body to extreme conditions might be attributable to the dense, fibre-like cytotardin meshwork.
source: We therefore anticipate that much of the resistance of the tardigrade body to extreme conditions, such as cryobiosis (Wright, 2001; Hengherr et al., 2009), might be attributable to the dense, fibre-like cytotardin meshwork.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the localization pattern and known functions of IF proteins.

claim: The belt-like structures encircling each epidermal cell might help to resist the shearing forces that arise during freezing and thawing cycles.
source: The belt-like structures encircling each epidermal cell might help to resist the shearing forces that arise during freezing and thawing cycles
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the functional role of cytotardin based on its structural arrangement.

claim: The dense meshwork at the basis of each claw and around the stylets might provide the tissue stability necessary for locomotion and feeding.
source: whereas the dense meshwork at the basis of each claw and around the stylets might provide the tissue stability necessary for locomotion and feeding.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the functional role of cytotardin based on its localization.

claim: Cytotardin of H. dujardini is a cytoplasmic IF protein, predominantly expressed in ectodermal epithelia, that has evolved independently from the cytoplasmic IF proteins of other bilaterians by gene duplication and subsequent neofunctionalization.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that cytotardin of H. dujardini is a cytoplasmic IF protein, predominantly expressed in ectodermal epithelia, that has evolved independently from the cytoplasmic IF proteins of other bilaterians by gene duplication and subsequent neofunctionalization (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is the main conclusion synthesizing phylogenetic, localization, and functional data.

claim: The evolution of cytotardin was most likely triggered by an initial loss of the CaaX motif and nuclear localization signal from the ancestral lamin gene in the tardigrade lineage.
source: This process was most likely triggered by an initial loss of the CaaX motif and nuclear localization signal from the ancestral lamin gene in the tardigrade lineage.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of these motifs in cytotardin and its cytoplasmic localization.

claim: Expression of the cytotardin protein in tissues that are subject to mechanical stress might have served as a pre-adaptation for the ability of tardigrades to survive extreme environmental conditions.
source: Expression of the cytotardin protein in tissues that are subject to mechanical stress might have served as a pre-adaptation for the ability of tardigrades to survive extreme environmental conditions.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the evolutionary significance of cytotardin.

claim: Similar duplication and neofunctionalization events might have occurred in the collembolan and copepod lineages.
source: Similar duplication and neofunctionalization events might have occurred in the collembolan and copepod lineages, as our findings demonstrate that these two taxa also show duplicated lamins that have lost their nuclear localization signals (Figures 3 and 6C and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analyses and domain predictions showing absence of NLS in certain collembolan and copepod lamin sequences.

claim: Isomin might stabilize the intestinal epithelial cells in collembolans.
source: While isomin might stabilize the intestinal epithelial cells in collembolans (Mencarelli et al., 2011)
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: Anti-lamin-1 antibody stains a band of approximately 70 kDa in H. dujardini lysates.
source: Anti-lamin-1 antibody stains a band of ≈70 kDa, as expected.
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Anti-lamin-2 antibody stains a band of approximately 72 kDa in H. dujardini lysates.
source: Anti-lamin-2 antibody stains a band of ≈72 kDa, as expected.
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Anti-cytotardin antibody stains a band of approximately 57 kDa in H. dujardini lysates, transformed E. coli, and transfected MCF-7 cells.
source: Anti-cytotardin antibody stains a band of ≈57 kDa, as expected.
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: H. dujardini specimens start with minuscule movements of one leg after 20 min of thawing and fully recover locomotion within 120 min after being frozen in ice for 4 days.
source: This time-lapse video shows thawing specimens of the tardigrade H. dujardini after 4 days frozen in ice. One specimen starts with minuscule movements of one leg after 20 min of thawing and fully recovers locomotion within 120 min.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Video 1.
